To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the DAE (2001) Report: (1) is based upon a model specification that is not consistent with the data; (2) contains an econometric specification error that is likely to have biased the estimated coefficients; and (3) contains a serious data error that is likely also to have biased the results.
the DAE (2008) Report is not a reliable guide to the economic benefits and/or costs of council amalgamation in Tasmania.

the DAE model: • Is based on a misspecified functional form, • Is misspecified because it fails to include an important explanatory variable, • Is misspecifed because it includes an irrelevant explanatory variable, • Fails to control for the effects of unobserved variables, • Contains errors in the data, • Is based on an inappropriate sample, • Fails the test for autocorrelation, • Fails an important diagnostic test, • Fails a test for heteroscedastic
In summary, our research is concerned with
the quality of evidence adduced in a major public policy document, which has been widely cited by the proponents of council amalgamations.
the quality of the evidence provided in the DAE Report and the extent to which the DAE Report is an example of the ‘hired gun’ phenomenon in action.
a particular instance of public policy making in Tasmania.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the DAE (2001) model does not support the case for radical local council amalgamations in Tasmania.
the econometric analysis in support of the Tasmanian amalgamation proposal is not robust.
there is no empirical evidence that the Tasmanian councils should amalgamate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the DAE Report is a poor piece of work that should not be used to support policy decisions.
the DAE (2001) Report provides a very weak case in support of amalgamation of Tasmainian local authorities.
DAE’s (2011) econometric analysis is not a reliable basis upon which to base public policy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the DAE (2009, 2010, 2011) Reports are not a reliable source of information on the economic effects of council mergers.
the econometric modelling employed in DAE (2010) is flawed, and that the DAE Report is not a credible source of evidence in favour of amalgamation.
it is imperative that the public policy process be open and transparent.
